input.strategy_title: Make RHOAI more usable for enterprise teams
input.strategy_markdown:
## Problem Statement

Several strategic accounts have told field teams that RHOAI "feels hard to use
at enterprise scale". Feedback arrived through different channels and has not
been consolidated; the quotes below are representative but partially
contradictory. Leadership wants visible usability progress this release.

## High-Level Requirements

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| HLR-1 | — | Administration should be simpler. One account wants fewer configuration options exposed ("too many knobs"), another explicitly wants more fine-grained controls per project. |
| HLR-2 | — | Onboarding a new data scientist should take "less than a day". It is not defined what onboarding includes or where the day is currently spent. |
| HLR-3 | — | The platform should "integrate better" with existing enterprise tooling. No specific tools were named in the consolidated feedback. |
| HLR-4 | P2 | Publish a whitepaper describing enterprise usability best practices on RHOAI. |

## Affected Components

- Dashboard
- Notebooks

## Out of Scope

Nothing has been explicitly scoped out.

## Open Questions

1. Which accounts' feedback takes precedence when requirements conflict (HLR-1)?
2. What does "onboarding" cover for HLR-2 — cluster access, project setup,
   first workbench, or first deployed model?
3. Which enterprise tools does HLR-3 actually mean?

# Resolve conflicting administration-experience requirements and set the configuration direction

## Description

The strategy's administration requirement is self-contradictory: one strategic
account wants fewer configuration options exposed ("too many knobs") while
another explicitly wants more fine-grained controls per project. The feedback
arrived through different channels, was never consolidated, and no precedence
rule exists. This investigation consolidates the account feedback, inventories
the administration configuration surface RHOAI exposes today, and obtains a
stakeholder-ratified decision on which direction the platform will pursue
(curated simplicity, per-project granularity, or a layered combination). Its
outcome determines which administration implementation epics exist and what
they do, and grounds the administration guidance in the enterprise usability
whitepaper.

## Scope

- Consolidate all administration-related feedback from strategic accounts and
  field channels into a single record with per-account attribution, surfacing
  every concrete statement about configuration complexity and control
  granularity.
- Inventory the administration configuration surface RHOAI exposes today:
  Dashboard-administered feature flags, platform defaults, and per-component
  settings (for example the OdhDashboardConfig-managed options, including
  workbench culling administration) — which knobs exist, where they are
  administered, and which are commonly used vs. rarely touched.
- Identify which accounts provided which requirement and the business weight
  behind each (account tier, renewal exposure, number of affected users).
- Draft a decision record presenting the bounded option set: (a) simplify by
  curating defaults and reducing exposed options, (b) add per-project
  fine-grained controls, (c) a layered approach that curates defaults while
  offering opt-in per-project granularity — with the trade-offs, migration
  impact on existing deployments, and effort profile of each.
- Obtain a stakeholder/product ruling on precedence and direction; record the
  decision, its rationale, and which requirement (if either) is declined or
  deferred.

## Acceptance Criteria

- All administration-related feedback from strategic accounts is consolidated
  into a single document with per-account attribution and source channel.
- A complete inventory of currently exposed administration configuration
  options exists, grouped by administering surface, with usage notes where
  available.
- A decision record is ratified by the product/stakeholder owners naming the
  chosen direction (simplify / per-project granularity / layered), with
  rationale and explicitly declined or deferred alternatives.
- The ratified decision identifies which downstream usability work is enabled,
  changed, or dropped as a result, in enough detail to scope implementation
  epics.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (administration should be simpler — conflicting account requirements):
  this investigation resolves the conflict that currently makes HLR-1
  unimplementable. Implementation epics are defined in a follow-up
  decomposition once the direction is ratified; the ratified direction and the
  consolidated feedback record also ground the whitepaper's administration
  guidance.

# Define data-scientist onboarding scope and baseline where onboarding time is spent today

## Description

The strategy sets a target — onboarding a new data scientist should take "less
than a day" — without defining what onboarding includes or measuring where the
day is currently spent. Until the scope is defined and the current state is
baselined, no implementation epic can be responsibly scoped: the fix differs
completely depending on whether the time goes to cluster access, project
setup, first workbench, or first deployed model. This investigation defines
the onboarding boundary, maps the current journey, and produces a per-stage
time breakdown with ranked bottlenecks. Its findings scope the phase-2
implementation epics and ground the onboarding best practices in the
enterprise usability whitepaper.

## Scope

- Obtain a ratified definition of what "onboarding a new data scientist"
  covers for the less-than-a-day target: which of cluster access, project
  setup, first workbench, and first deployed model count as onboarding (a
  product decision, recorded with rationale).
- Map the current end-to-end onboarding journey as a new data scientist
  experiences it — from account/project request through project creation in
  the Dashboard console, workbench spawn, and first productive notebook
  session — identifying the responsible platform surface for each stage
  (Dashboard console, Notebooks/workbench tooling, customer-side or
  platform-side administration).
- Measure or estimate the current time spent per stage, based on the
  documented flow, walkthroughs of a representative environment, and field
  feedback, and rank the bottlenecks (wait time vs. manual steps vs.
  comprehension/learning time).
- Distinguish friction that is within platform control from friction that is
  external (customer-side approvals, cluster capacity, procurement).
- Produce a findings report: the ratified onboarding scope, the per-stage time
  breakdown, the ranked bottlenecks, and candidate improvement areas with the
  affected platform surface for each — suitable for scoping implementation
  epics.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A ratified definition of the onboarding scope exists, stating which stages
  (cluster access, project setup, first workbench, first deployed model) count
  toward the less-than-a-day target.
- The current onboarding journey is documented stage by stage, with the
  responsible platform surface or external party identified for each stage.
- A per-stage time breakdown exists for the current state, with the dominant
  bottleneck(s) identified and the evidence for each figure recorded.
- The findings explicitly separate platform-controllable friction from
  external/customer-side friction.
- Candidate improvement areas are enumerated, each tagged with the platform
  surface it would touch, in enough detail to scope implementation epics.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 (onboarding a new data scientist should take less than a day — scope
  undefined): this investigation defines the scope and baselines the current
  state that HLR-2's target is measured against. Implementation epics are
  defined in a follow-up decomposition against the ranked bottlenecks; the
  findings also ground the whitepaper's onboarding guidance.

# Identify and prioritize the enterprise tools behind the integration feedback

## Description

The strategy asks that RHOAI "integrate better" with existing enterprise
tooling, but no specific tools were named in the consolidated feedback. The
target tool set determines everything downstream: which components and teams
the integration work touches, whether it is authentication, source control,
CI, ticketing, data platforms, or ML tooling, and whether the work is even on
the affected components listed in the strategy. This investigation names the
tools, weighs the demand behind each, inventories RHOAI's existing integration
points, and produces a prioritized, ratified target-tool list. Its outcome
determines which integration implementation epics exist and what they do, and
grounds the enterprise-tooling guidance in the usability whitepaper.

## Scope

- Consolidate all integration-related feedback from strategic accounts and
  field channels into a single record with per-account attribution, extracting
  every concrete tool or system mention.
- Engage field teams and account owners to name the specific enterprise tools
  behind the general "integrate better" statements (for example: identity
  providers, source control, CI systems, ticketing/work management, data
  platforms, model/ML tooling), since the consolidated feedback names none.
- Inventory RHOAI's existing enterprise integration points (for example
  OpenShift OAuth for authentication and project-scoped RBAC, workbench source
  control integration) from the platform's documentation and architecture
  context, and identify the gaps relative to the named tools.
- For each candidate tool, assess demand weight (how many accounts, which
  strategic accounts), the rough integration surface, and the platform
  component that would primarily own the work.
- Produce a prioritized target-tool list, ratified by product/stakeholder
  owners, with per-tool rationale, demand evidence, and the platform surface
  each integration would touch.

## Acceptance Criteria

- All integration-related feedback is consolidated into a single document with
  per-account attribution and any concrete tool mentions extracted.
- A named candidate tool list exists with per-account demand evidence and a
  rough integration surface assessment for each tool.
- RHOAI's existing enterprise integration points are inventoried, with gaps
  identified relative to the named tools.
- A prioritized target-tool list is ratified by product/stakeholder owners,
  identifying for each tool the platform component the integration would
  primarily touch — in enough detail to scope implementation epics.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (the platform should integrate better with existing enterprise
  tooling — no tools named): this investigation resolves which tools HLR-3
  actually refers to. Implementation epics are defined in a follow-up
  decomposition once the target tools are ratified; the prioritized list also
  grounds the whitepaper's enterprise-tooling guidance.

# Publish the enterprise usability best-practices whitepaper for RHOAI

## Description

Author and publish a Red Hat whitepaper describing enterprise usability best
practices on RHOAI, covering administration and configuration governance,
data-scientist onboarding, and enterprise tooling integration. The content is
written after the enterprise-usability direction is resolved — the ratified
administration-configuration direction, the defined onboarding scope with its
time baseline, and the named enterprise tooling targets — so that published
guidance matches the platform's chosen direction rather than restating the
contradictory raw account feedback the strategy starts from.

## Scope

- Content outline for the whitepaper, covering:
  - administration and configuration governance practices, aligned with the
    ratified configuration direction (curated simplicity, per-project
    granularity, or layered);
  - data-scientist onboarding practices, aligned with the defined onboarding
    scope and its measured per-stage baseline;
  - enterprise tooling integration practices, aligned with the named and
    prioritized target tools.
- Author the whitepaper through the Red Hat docs/content process.
- Technically review the content against RHOAI's architecture context (the
    Dashboard and Notebooks components) and current documented platform
    behavior; record review sign-off.
- Publish the whitepaper and record the publication reference.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A reviewed and approved content outline exists covering the three practice
  areas (administration, onboarding, enterprise tooling integration).
- The administration/configuration guidance is consistent with the ratified
  configuration direction and does not present contradictory guidance on
  configuration granularity.
- The onboarding and integration guidance reflects the defined onboarding
  scope and the ratified target-tool list, respectively.
- The content is technically reviewed against the platform's architecture
  context and current documented behavior, with review sign-off recorded.
- The whitepaper is published through the Red Hat content process, with the
  publication reference recorded.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-4 (P2 — publish a whitepaper describing enterprise usability best
  practices on RHOAI): direct coverage — the whitepaper is outlined, authored,
  technically reviewed, and published. Content accuracy draws on the resolved
  outcomes of the HLR-1, HLR-2, and HLR-3 investigations.

# Decomposition Summary — RHAISTRAT-9008: Make RHOAI more usable for enterprise teams

## Approach

This strategy is not implementable as written: HLR-1 states two contradictory
requirements (fewer exposed configuration options vs. more fine-grained
per-project controls), HLR-2 sets a target ("onboarding in less than a day")
without defining what onboarding covers or where the time is spent today, and
HLR-3 asks for "better integration" with enterprise tooling without naming a
single tool. All three carry explicit open questions in the strategy, and each
answer changes which implementation epics exist and what they do. None of the
three names a target state or measurable criteria, so writing implementation
epics for them now would require inventing scope the strategy does not contain.

Per the unbounded-outcome path of the investigation-edge rule, this is a
**phased (investigation-first) decomposition**:

- **Phase 1 (this decomposition):** one Investigation epic per genuine unknown
  (HLR-1, HLR-2, HLR-3), plus the one fully specified deliverable — the HLR-4
  whitepaper (`docs-authoring`), which consumes the investigations' findings so
  published guidance matches the resolved direction instead of the contradictory
  raw feedback.
- **Phase 2 (follow-up decomposition after the investigations resolve):**
  implementation epics for HLR-1..HLR-3, scoped from the ratified decisions.

No Staff Engineer Input section is present in the strategy; no overrides to log.

## Epic List

| ID | Title | Type | Team | Priority |
|----|-------|------|------|----------|
| RHAISTRAT-9008-E001 | Resolve conflicting administration-experience requirements and set the configuration direction | Investigation | RHOAI Dashboard | P1 |
| RHAISTRAT-9008-E002 | Define data-scientist onboarding scope and baseline where onboarding time is spent today | Investigation | RHOAI Dashboard | P1 |
| RHAISTRAT-9008-E003 | Identify and prioritize the enterprise tools behind the integration feedback | Investigation | RHOAI Dashboard | P1 |
| RHAISTRAT-9008-E004 | Publish the enterprise usability best-practices whitepaper for RHOAI | Implementation (docs-authoring) | RHOAI Documentation | P2 |

## Dependency DAG

```mermaid
graph TD
    E001[RHAISTRAT-9008-E001] --> E004[RHAISTRAT-9008-E004]
    E002[RHAISTRAT-9008-E002] --> E004
    E003[RHAISTRAT-9008-E003] --> E004
```

All three Investigations are roots and run in parallel. The whitepaper is the
only downstream node.

## DAG Justification

| Edge | Rule | Rationale |
|------|------|-----------|
| E001 → E004 | Investigation gates downstream work (Rule 3); artifact consumption | The whitepaper's administration/configuration guidance cannot be written while the platform direction is self-contradictory (curated simplicity vs. per-project granularity). The administration-direction investigation produces the consolidated feedback record and ratified decision the whitepaper's guidance builds on. This is the epic's primary gate: `gated_by=E001`, `gate_failure_impact.action=rewrite` — if the direction decision changes or is not ratified, the administration sections are rewritten to match. |
| E002 → E004 | Investigation gates downstream work (Rule 3); artifact consumption | The onboarding best-practice sections require the defined onboarding scope and the per-stage time baseline this investigation produces; without them the whitepaper would prescribe practices for an undefined journey. |
| E003 → E004 | Investigation gates downstream work (Rule 3); artifact consumption | The enterprise-tooling integration guidance requires the named, prioritized target tools this investigation produces; the strategy names none. |

Notes on the graph:

- `gated_by` is single-valued in the schema; it records the primary gate (E001,
  the direction decision that most rewrites whitepaper content). E002 and E003
  are additional investigation dependencies of E004 — artifact-consumption
  edges of the same Rule 3 kind.
- There are no implementation-to-implementation edges because this phase
  contains no implementation epics for HLR-1..HLR-3 (see Approach).
- No Rule 11 (docs-last) edges are required: the strategy's only
  Implementation epic is itself the `docs-authoring` epic. When the phase-2
  implementation epics are created, they must be added to the whitepaper's
  blockers before publication (see Health Warnings).
- No parallelism rules for `repo-onboarding` / `konflux-onboarding` /
  `license-validation` apply: both affected components (Dashboard, Notebooks)
  exist in architecture context and are Konflux-onboarded; no new component is
  introduced.

## HLR Traceability Matrix

| HLR | Priority (strategy) | Epic(s) | Coverage |
|-----|---------------------|---------|----------|
| HLR-1 — Administration should be simpler (contradictory: fewer knobs vs. more granular controls) | — (unassigned) | RHAISTRAT-9008-E001 | Investigation resolves the conflict and ratifies a direction; implementation epics are cut in the phase-2 decomposition once the direction is decided. |
| HLR-2 — Onboarding a new data scientist in less than a day (scope undefined) | — (unassigned) | RHAISTRAT-9008-E002 | Investigation defines the onboarding scope and baselines current time per stage; implementation epics follow in phase 2 against the measured bottlenecks. |
| HLR-3 — Better integration with existing enterprise tooling (no tools named) | — (unassigned) | RHAISTRAT-9008-E003 | Investigation names and prioritizes the target tools and the platform surface each touches; implementation epics follow in phase 2. |
| HLR-4 — Publish a whitepaper describing enterprise usability best practices on RHOAI | P2 | RHAISTRAT-9008-E004 | Direct coverage: the whitepaper is authored and published through the Red Hat content process. |

All four HLRs are covered; none is orphaned. HLR-1..HLR-3 are covered by the
investigation that unblocks them (their implementation work does not exist as
epics in this phase by design — see Approach), and each investigation's
findings feed the whitepaper.

## Health Warnings

1. **Missing strategy sections.** The strategy has no Impacted Teams table, no
   Dependencies table, no Acceptance Criteria (Given/When/Then), no
   Non-Functional Requirements, no Staff Engineer Input, and no per-component
   change/owner detail in the Affected Components list. Owner teams were
   inferred from architecture context (Dashboard → RHOAI Dashboard; Notebooks →
   Workbenches); the whitepaper team ("RHOAI Documentation") is an assumption —
   confirm before scheduling.
2. **Unassigned HLR priorities.** HLR-1..HLR-3 carry no priority in the
   strategy. The three Investigations are set to P1 as the critical path to any
   usability progress (the strategy's overall priority is Normal and leadership
   wants visible progress this release). Confirm with product.
3. **Self-contradictory requirement (HLR-1).** "Fewer configuration options
   exposed" and "more fine-grained controls per project" pull in opposite
   directions. Escalated to an Investigation rather than arbitrarily picking a
   side; the resolution is a stakeholder decision, not a technical one.
4. **Scope trap.** "Nothing has been explicitly scoped out" combined with
   undefined scope for HLR-2 and HLR-3 risks unbounded scope growth. The
   investigations bound the scope before any implementation epic is cut.
5. **Priority-inversion risk.** HLR-4 (the P2 whitepaper) is the only
   prioritized requirement while the substantive usability work is
   unprioritized and blocked on unresolved questions. Publishing the whitepaper
   must not be treated as the release's "visible usability progress" while
   HLR-1..HLR-3 remain unimplemented.
6. **Source-data quality.** The feedback arrived through different channels and
   was never consolidated, and the quotes are "partially contradictory". All
   three investigations depend on this unconsolidated input; consolidation is
   part of each investigation's scope.
7. **Phase-2 Rule 11 obligation.** When the follow-up decomposition creates
   implementation epics for HLR-1..HLR-3, those epics must be added to the
   whitepaper epic's dependency chain before publication (docs describe what
   was built).
8. **Component mapping notes.** The onboarding investigation spans Dashboard
   and Notebooks; it is assigned to Dashboard (canonical component, RHOAI
   Dashboard team) as the console through which the whole onboarding journey
   runs, with Workbenches/Notebooks as a noted span. The tooling investigation
   is assigned to Dashboard because the Dashboard architecture context makes it
